This paper investigates inference-time computation strategies to enhance the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs). The authors provide an extensive empirical study (1,000+ experiments over 20,000 A100-80G GPU hours) evaluating six inference-time computation methods across eight reasoning tasks. Key variables studied include instruction prompting styles, temperature, top-p sampling, and reward models. The authors introduce a benchmark framework and find that simple yet often-overlooked techniques like prompt type and sampling hyperparameters can have a significant impact on performance. The study offers insights into combining various techniques and emphasizes reproducibility with open-sourced code.

Strengths
- Comprehensive and systematic empirical study with large compute budget and diverse tasks/models.
- Clear ablation isolating effects of prompts, hyperparams and reward models.
- It Establishes standardized benchmark and public codebase

(c) Weaknesses
- Many of the findings are well known
- Limited efficiency metrics beyond token counts; cost-effectiveness and FLOPs not fully analyzed.
- Combination of techniques underexplored; guidance for practitioners remains limited

During the rebuttal, authors clarified some of the concerns including token-based efficiency as proxy for FLOPs, and added error breakdowns. Although concerns on the cost analysis and combination of multiple tricks remain, the paper's contribution is solid and outweighs its limitations.

Dear Reviewer o2dp,

Thank you for your thoughtful follow-up and for recognizing that most of your earlier concerns have been addressed. We greatly appreciate your additional, concrete suggestions regarding more comprehensive trick-stacking evaluations,  LRM coverage, and reproducibility improvements. We would like to share our planned next steps as our future work.

1.  Expanded trick-stacking results.
We will substantially extend the evaluation in §4.2.3 and Table 3 by moving beyond the current limited set of combinations to a more systematic exploration. Specifically, we will perform a full temperature–top-p grid search (e.g., temperature ∈ {0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0}, top-p ∈ {0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 1.0}) to map their joint effects, layer these sampling settings with diverse prompting strategies (e.g., CoT, Reflect CoT, verification-based prompting) and reward models (e.g., majority vote, self-evaluation, domain-specific PRMs), and test multi-layer stackings rather than mostly pairwise combinations. Results will be visualized as interaction heatmaps and analyzed per task type to identify robust “golden combinations” and failure cases, providing deeper, actionable insights beyond confirming common knowledge.

2. Additional LRM evaluation.
We commit to adding a much more comprehensive evaluation of LRMs. Specifically, we will incorporate experiments on representative Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), such as DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-o1, to directly examine the transferability and limitations of the proposed techniques in reasoning-specialized settings. This will include both standalone results and comparative analysis with general-purpose LLMs, addressing the dynamic differences you highlighted.

3. Reproducibility enhancements.
Following your recommendations and prior work \[2,3], we will provide FP32 decoding results for greedy sampling alongside FP16 runs, and include “average of N” vs. “best of N” comparisons. This will help quantify the variance introduced by hardware/serving setups and sampling randomness, ensuring greater reproducibility.

We believe these additions will meaningfully strengthen the paper and more directly address your W1 and F2 points, while also improving evaluation stability and transparency. Thank you again for your valuable guidance. We look forward to incorporating these improvements into the final version.

Best regards,

The Authors

**I appreciate the rebuttal and find most concerns addressed or clarified.** 

However, I do find the response regarding W1 (not enough trick-stacking results) and F2 (LRM coverage) a bit hand-wavy, as I believe a faithful author would agree that:

- Most takeaways from `L277` indeed remain common knowledge of the field. While some of them are more intricate, most of such "more intricate" insights — e.g., regulating general-purpose LLMs to engage in reasoning tasks with a reasoning PRM — are likely built upon an outdated setup, given the popularity of LRMs. Thus, although it is nice that we can now have quantitative + comprehensive evidence to support such common understandings, I do like to see more trick-stacking results beyond  §4.2.3 and Table 3 — which are not provided here.
- There are significant dynamic differences between a general-purpose LLM and its reasoning counterparts (one good example is how DeepSeek-R1 is less friendly to few-shot examples), let alone considering how such reasoning capabilities are enabled. LRM also has many specific TTC methods adopted under a reasoning context — for instance, those which featured in Table 4 of [1] — and likely require much more engaged investigation to reach any conclusion as solid as the rest of the paper. In other words, while many presented techniques are technically model-agnostic, many of them will not be realistically transferred, and the conclusions we shall reach upon those techniques might change.

I therefore recommend that the authors:

1. Committing to adding a much more comprehensive evaluation of LRMs,
2. Or alternatively, strictly position this as a non-reasoning LLM-only work.

Additionally, as an extension of F1, it might be worth noting that 16-bit decoding under greedy sampling brings much variance just by changing the hardware/serving setup, so it is recommended to reproduce greedy runs under FP32 for improved consistency (see [2] for more details; as well as lossless efficiency art like [3]). [2] also — though in this case rather unsurprisingly — suggests temperature sampling bring much randomness beyond numerical stability issues, where multiple FP16 runs are preferred (which I assume the authors are already doing). However, such fluctuation suggests it might be helpful to have some "average of N" results to contrast with "best of N." 

May the authors please share their next steps regarding this work?

---
[1] Stop Overthinking: A Survey on Efficient Reasoning for Large Language Models   
[2] Give Me FP32 or Give Me Death? Challenges and Solutions for Reproducible Reasoning   
[3] Break the Sequential Dependency of LLM Inference Using Lookahead Decoding

We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewer for the constructive feedback and for raising the score. We greatly appreciate the recognition and will carefully incorporate the suggestions to strengthen the cost/efficiency analysis, explore more effective combinations of techniques, enhance the visualizations, and include the thorough error analysis in future versions of the paper.

**Regarding FLOPs-per-token vs. Generation Compute**  We apologize for any confusion. We should have been clearer: our reported output-token statistic includes all candidate tokens generated by the model, rather than only the final response presented to the user. We understand that this distinction was not stated explicitly in the paper and may have led to misunderstanding. 

As stated in the literature[2, 4], there are generally two ways to report computational cost:

1. **FLOPs-per-token**  following OpenAI’s scaling-laws formulation \[1] Table 1, where the forward pass of decoder-only Transformers involves approximately

$$
C_{\text{forward}} \approx 2N + 2n_{\text{layer}}n_{\text{ctx}}d_{\text{attn}},
$$

with $N = 2d_{\text{model}}n_{\text{layer}}(2d_{\text{attn}}+d_{\text{ff}}) $ denoting the number of non-embedding parameters \[1,4].

2. **Generation compute** the total number of computations generation, i.e., the average number of tokens generated at the sentence level together with the average number of forward computations at the token level for solving one problem \[3].

In our setting, $n_{\text{layer}}$, $d_{\text{model}}$, $d_{\text{attn}}$, $d_{\text{ff}}$, and $n_{\text{ctx}}$ are fixed. Therefore, $C_{\text{forward}}$ is constant for a given model, and:

$\text{Generation Compute}= (\text{ *generated tokens})\times C_{\text{forward}}.$

This shows that, under fixed model architecture and context length, **generation compute is proportional to FLOPs-per-token**. The difference lies in the counting scope: generation compute includes *all candidate tokens generated during in inference*, not only the final user-facing output, thereby capturing the actual inference workload in our evaluation.

We acknowledge that this distinction was not made explicit in the original submission and will revise the manuscript to clearly state that our efficiency analysis is based on the generation compute definition.

\[1] Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, 2020

\[2] Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, 2022

\[3] AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training, ICML 2024

\[4] Hugging Face, Understanding FLOPs-per-token estimates from OpenAI’s scaling laws, 2022.

### Thanks for Reviewer 2cZo and global response

We sincerely thank Reviewer 2cZo for the exceptionally detailed, constructive, and thoughtful review. This is truly one of the most insightful and high-quality reviews we have received, and we deeply appreciate the time and expertise the reviewer has dedicated to understanding and evaluating our work.

We are particularly grateful for the recognition of:

* the **extensive empirical evaluation** (1,000+ runs over 20,000 A100 GPU hours),
* the **practical relevance** of inference-time computation strategies under increasingly complex reasoning settings, and
* the **value of our findings**, especially the strength of self-consistency and the nuanced impact of inference-time hyperparameters.

We also deeply appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestions regarding **clarity of organization**, **novelty framing**, and **possible follow-up analyses** (e.g., weighted voting, reward aggregation, and further cross-method comparisons). These comments have helped us identify areas for improvement and expansion in our revision.

Below, we provide a point-by-point response. We thank the reviewer again for this outstanding feedback, which will greatly improve the clarity, depth, and impact of our final version.

> L2:  "The novelty is a bit limited. While the benchmarking effort is valuable, the paper largely feels like a systematic sweep of known techniques and hyperparameters (prompt styles, search techniques, reward types). The impact of temperature, for instance, is already generally understood in the community."

Response: While some individual findings (e.g., the effectiveness of CoT prompts or the role of temperature) may align with community intuition, our contribution lies in their comprehensive empirical validation and joint analysis across diverse tasks and model families. Specifically:
* Providing the first large-scale empirical comparison (20,000+ GPU hours, 1,000+ configurations) across decoding strategies, post-hoc rewriting, and reward models, revealing non-trivial interactions (e.g., self-correction undermining reward-based decoding).
*  Providing systematic empirical insights into often-overlooked inference-time configurations, such as sampling hyperparameters, prompt types, and reward model choices. 
* Highlighting failure modes and incompatibilities between methods, and offering practical design heuristics for combining inference-time techniques (e.g., when not to pair high-variance strategies).
* Identifying and empirically validating the lack of generalization in reward-model-based decoding, a behavior previously hypothesized but not analyzed in detail.
* In addition, one of our key findings is that self-evaluation often fails to yield reliable improvements across tasks. This contrasts with several prior works that rely on LLMs to evaluate or guide their own outputs. Our results suggest that such self-evaluation approaches may be limited in practice and warrant more careful analysis.

> L3: "There could have some investigation of self-consistency with weighted voting (e.g. based on some normalized score from different reward models) or other methods. If all the samples are recorded, this could have been done without new experiments."

Response: Thank you for the insightful suggestion. We conducted an additional experiment using weighted self-consistency based on reward signals. While the overall improvements are modest, we did observe slight gains on math-related tasks, such as MATH and GSM-HARD. We will incorporate these results into a future revision.

| Model      | Method                     | HumanEval | GSM8K     | GSM-HARD | MATH     | PrOntoQ   |
|------------|----------------------------|-----------|----------|----------|----------|-----------|
| Llama-8b   | Weighted Self-Consistency  | 59.1/1261 | 85.4/976 | 35.0/1174| 46.4/1412| 93.1/969  |
| Qwen-7b    | Weighted Self-Consistency  | 79.3/1271 | 91.5/1462| 51.1/1174| 70.7/1878| 94.9/1271 |




> Q1: “ It seems self-consistency performs surprisingly well compared to more sophisticated methods like MCTS. Why is this not more strongly emphasized?”

We believe the performance gap can be partially explained by limitations in reward model generalization. As we discuss in Section 4.2.2 and visualize in Figure 7, reward models (especially in complex tasks like MATH) often suffer from miscalibration and overfit to superficial patterns, leading to suboptimal or inflated selection during inference. In contrast, self-consistency sidesteps these issues by leveraging the natural redundancy of correct reasoning paths: correct answers tend to emerge more frequently when sampling from a well-calibrated LLM.
To better reflect this insight, we will revise the conclusion and takeaway sections to explicitly highlight self-consistency’s strengths. 

> Q2: "Which variant of beam search is used? Is it step-wise beam search like in Xie et al. (2023)?"

Yes, we follow the step-wise beam search formulation as in Xie et al. (NeurIPS 2023). At each reasoning step, the beam expands candidate continuations and prunes them based on scores to maintain the most promising trajectories. However, in contrast to Xie et al., who utilize self-evaluation, we replace self-evaluation with a consistent, model-agnostic reward signal: the RLHF reward model, as described in our Section 4.3 benchmark setup to ensure the fair comparison.

> Q3: "Does your MCTS involve reward-weighted aggregation like in Hao et al. (2023)?"

Yes. We follow the standard UCT formulation as described in Luo et al. [1], which aligns with the approach used in Hao et al. regarding the MCTS process. The reward signal used during the playouts is derived from QwQ-32B, as detailed in Section 4.3.

[1] Luo et al. Improve mathematical reasoning in language models by automated process supervision. arXiv:2406.06592, 2024.


> [W1 & F1]: "Definitions like Reflect-CoT are hard to find; could they be brought closer to the main content?"

Thank you for this suggestion. We will revise the main text to include brief in-line definitions of Reflect-CoT and related prompt types where they are first introduced, while still referring to the appendix for extended examples.

> F2: "Could the hyperparameter search space be more explicitly listed?"

In the revised version, we will include a table of the hyperparameter ranges (e.g., temperature: 0.6–1.0, top-p: 0.6–1.0, N: 1–16) in the appendix for each set of experiments, to improve clarity and reproducibility.

> F3:" Takeaways can be more section-specific, and highlight what findings are novel."

We appreciate this feedback. In the revised version, we will add takeaways in each experiment section to clarify our conclusions.

> F4: "So what could have went wrong on the previous approaches? Poor temperature or something else?"

We suggest that one key issue lies in the generalization limitations of reward models, particularly when used in complex or step-level inference strategies. As highlighted in our findings (Takeaway #5), reward models can inflate performance evaluations, often favoring superficially plausible answers over genuinely correct ones. This leads to inconsistent task performance, especially in math and code reasoning domains.

In methods that depend heavily on reward guidance, such as step-wise beam search or MCTS, the overall effectiveness becomes tightly coupled with the reliability and calibration of the reward model. As shown in Table 2, even sophisticated techniques can underperform when paired with misaligned or brittle reward functions. This may explain why some prior works, despite their algorithmic complexity, fail to consistently outperform simpler baselines like self-consistency, which operate independently of external reward signals.

summary.value: This paper present a comprehensive benchmark of inference-time tricks for language models.

strengths_contributions.value:
* LLMs have many knobs to tune, yet typical evaluations of non-reasoning LLMs still rely on vanilla greedy decoding, which is unreflective. This paper properly exposes how those knobs affect performance.

* Good task coverage.

* Very fine-grained sweeps for each contributing factor.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
* Most takeaways in `L277` are rather intuitive and already common knowledge in the field. My main interest is how the tricks **stack**; on this front, only a brief §4.2.3 and a small Table 3 appear—leaving much to be desired. The authors should expand this analysis, especially for closely related knobs (e.g., temperature - top-p grid search).

* Visualization readability can improve. Results are shown as bar charts (per dataset) or line graphs (per setting), yet no averages are reported, making it hard to link the claimed insights to the plots. For example, Takeaway 1 and the text around `L202` assert CoT’s superiority, but Figure 2 does not make this obvious. Please add an average column to each chart—and, more importantly, an averaged line or column across each figure set.

* No real efficiency report.

I find this work helpful and appreciate the effort of running comprehensive experiments. Should the author be able to address my concerns, I am willing to improve my ratings.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
- For models under random sampling, just running the same task twice with different random seeds can yield different results. How many runs did the authors do for non-greedy evaluations?
- Why is there no feature of reasoning models? Most of the tricks featured can be adopted to LRMs.

final_justification.value:
The authors has addressed most of my concerns except the additional experiments request regarding trick stacking and LRMs, which are both promised to be included in the updated version.

I believe the work is of 4-ish quality even without the LRM portion. Granted such additional experiments are generally of no risk but just of resource needs, I am preemptively issuing a 5.

summary.value: This paper systematically investigates and benchmarks various inference-time computation techniques to improve the reasoning capabilities of LLMs without modifying their parameters or requiring extra training. It focuses on tuning generation strategies (e.g., prompt types, temperature, top-p) and solution selection mechanisms (e.g., reward models, self-evaluation) to enhance performance across a wide set of reasoning tasks.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper evaluates multiple inference-time methods across multiple datasets
2. This paper gives ablation study to demonstrates that prompt choice, temperature, and top-p tuning can significantly improve reasoning performance.
3. This paper proposes for lightweight and accessible techniques in practice.
4. This paper analyzes the effectiveness and limitations of reward models.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper provides empirical results but offers limited theoretical insight into why certain tricks work so effectively. It focuses on empirical results without delving into the underlying mechanisms driving performance gains. 
2. As mentioned in Section 6, the inference-time tricks are highly task-specific. I was wondering if that will limit plug-and-play generalization in practice.
3. Although the tricks are said to be low-cost, the paper does not provide any analysis of runtime, latency, or token budget implications, especially important when longer or repeated prompts are used.

summary.value:
The paper compares different LLMs on different datasets (HumanEval, MATH, GSM8K etc.) on two main aspects:

1. Solution Candidate Generation (step-wise or global):

Which involdes techniques - like hyperparameter differences (Top P, temperature) and prompts (COT, COT + reflection etc.) and such

2. Optimal Solution Selection:

Which involves techniques like Beam Search, MCTS, Self-consistency, Best-of-N, and other elements like reward types (self-evaluation, process-reward model etc.).  


The paper discovers some overlooked choices like temperature can have a significant affect, and provides several takeaways and recommendations based on the benchmarks.

strengths_contributions.value:
* Extensive evaluation of methods.
* Very relevant topic given the trendiness of interence-time scaling, and the huge array of methods and degree of freedom for inference-time-scaling - often lacking exhaustive benchmark and clear guidelines.
* There seems to be some interesting findings. Most striking to me (Figure 8) (if I am understanding the results correctly) (although not as emphasized in the paper), is how strongly plain self-consistency seems to perform -- which seems to put to question why more sophistical methods or separate reward models need to be used.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
* I found the paper a bit hard to track. Perhaps, the organization can be improved a bit. (see feedback)
* The novelty is a bit limited. While of course, as a benchmark paper, I am not talking about novelty in models - but loosely speaking, even in case of benchmarking there can be aspects of novelty like construction of new bencmarks, new evaluation methodologies, or even framing the benchmarkiing in some novel ways and getting novel insights. This paper feels more like a systematic hyperparameter sweep on some standard variables (prompt styles, search techniques, reward types). The paper emphasizes on the finding of the impact of temperature - but my impression is that temperature is generally understood as an impactful variable - as a background knowledge; and temperature like 0.7-0.8 seems already the standard for Self-consistency style use - because of need of diversity, but balancing with coherence. Nevertheless, this study is still very useful to have when done so extensively, and the effort in this is commendable (as such, I still lean towards acceptance personally), but I am still making this point explicit for consideration of meta-review. 
* There could have some investigation of self-consistency with weighted voting (e.g. based on some normalized score from different reward models) or other methods. If all the samples are recorded, this could have been done without new experiments.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
Feedback:

* Some of the important terminological definitions like Reflect COT is in the appendix - and could benefit from being more easily findable proximate to where the terms are used, or from the preliminary (even if citing to the appendix). 
* Perhaps more explicitly the search space of the hyperparameters (in a table or json like format) per section/experiment set could be presented in the appendix.
* Could add some dedicated takeaway for each of the main sections (rather than just the last)


**Takeways**

Regarding takeaways, I think the paper can be improve if it emphasizes and capitalizes better on which part of its findings is novel - and perhaps challenges the orthodox understanding (if any) - especially in the takeaway points. 


Also, If I am getting this right, it terms of solution selection, plain self-consistency seems to be still very strong:
* With the possibility of caching and concurrency, it can be very efficient and fast compared to others (Beam Search/MCTS or iterative solutions)
* Does not require any separate model
* Still seems to be beating most of the other more sophisticated model. 

If so, this can be better emphasized. 

If this is true, then there can be also further discussion in comparison to prior works. Self-Consistency is an old strategy, and I would assume most new strategies seem to use self-consistency as a baseline (well atleast some of them did  - not as familiar with recent developtments) e.g.  

Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model - Hao et al. EMNLP 2023 (Table 2). 
Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search for Reasoning - Xie et al. NeurIPS 2023 

So what could have went wrong on the previous approaches? Poor temperature or something else?

There seems to be also some related overlaps with this paper (even if the search space of techniques are different): Zero-Shot Verification-guided Chain of Thoughts - Ray Chowdhury ArXiv 2025 - on comparing stepwise greedy (stepwise best-of-N), beam search, self consistency, with different prompts -- also seem to have a similar finding of self-consistency + majority voting as a strong approach hard to beat. 

**question**

* Which version of beam-search is exactly used? For instance (Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search for Reasoning - Xie et al. NeurIPS 2023 ) has a step-wise beam search (which can be used with other reward types) instead of a traditional token-wise beam search. Was this considered?
* Does your MCTS use any kind of aggregation like weighted voting similar to (Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model - Hao et al. EMNLP 2023)?

title.value: Bag of Tricks for Inference-time Computation of LLM Reasoning

abstract.value: With the advancement of large language models (LLMs), solving complex tasks (e.g., math problems, code generation, etc.) has garnered increasing attention. Inference-time computation methods (e.g., Best-of-N, MCTS, etc.) are of significant importance, as they have the potential to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs without requiring external training computation. However, due to the inherent challenges of this technique, most existing methods remain proof-of-concept and are not yet sufficiently effective. In this paper, we investigate and benchmark strategies for improving inference-time computation across a wide range of reasoning tasks. Since most current methods rely on a pipeline that first generates candidate solutions (e.g., generating chain-of-thought candidate solutions) and then selects them based on specific reward signals (e.g., RLHF reward, process reward, etc.), our research focuses on strategies for both candidate solution generation (e.g., instructing prompts, hyperparameters: temperature and top-p, etc.) and reward mechanisms (e.g., self-evaluation, reward types, etc.). The experimental results reveal that several previously overlooked strategies can be critical for the success of inference-time computation (e.g., simplifying the temperature can improve general reasoning task performance by up to 5%). Based on extensive experiments (more than 20,000 A100-80G GPU hours with over 1,000 experiments) across a variety of models (e.g., Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families) of various sizes, our proposed strategies outperform the baseline by a substantial margin in most cases, providing a stronger foundation for future research.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).
